claims.claim: Prepositions are relationship words: they show a relationship in space, in time, or a logical relationship between people, places, or things, and they are most commonly followed by a noun phrase.
A prepositional phrase consists of a preposition plus its object (most often a noun phrase), and the whole phrase functions as a modifier, acting like an adjective or an adverb.

For place, at treats a location as a point or exact position (at the entrance, at 15 Craig Street), on marks a surface (on the counter) and is also used with buses, trains, and planes, and in marks an enclosed space or area (in the fridge, in a city, in a car).

For time, at is used with clock times and particular moments (at noon, at midnight), on with days and dates (on Friday, on 19 October), and in with months, years, seasons, and parts of the day (in December, in 2026, in spring, in the evening).

Prepositions of direction and movement include to (movement toward a destination), from (the starting point), into (movement toward the interior of a space), out of (movement from inside to outside), across (movement over or to the other side of a surface or line), and through (movement through a space); direction prepositions typically appear with verbs of motion, while location prepositions appear with state verbs such as be.

Verb + preposition combinations such as depend on, listen to, rely on, and wait for are fixed patterns: there are no grammatical rules that predict which preposition follows which verb, so the combinations are learned together as units.

Preposition errors are common among learners because preposition systems differ across languages; some languages do not use prepositions at all, so the choice must be learned per language rather than translated.

Ending a sentence with a preposition is permissible in English; the traditional prohibition traces to seventeenth-century writers (notably Joshua Poole and John Dryden) who wanted English grammar to match Latin, and although many style guides still avoid sentence-final prepositions in formal writing, the guideline is a stylistic convention rather than a rule of grammar.

A phrasal verb is a multi-word verb made of a main verb and at least one preposition or particle that changes the meaning of the verb (for example, turn off); phrasal verbs are a separate topic from prepositions themselves.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Ending a sentence with a preposition: error or not?
positions: Traditional formal-writing guidance treats a sentence-final preposition (preposition stranding) as something to avoid, and some style guides still advise rephrasing (This is the tool with which we work).

Modern usage reference (Merriam-Webster) states that ending a sentence with a preposition is permissible in English; the prohibition originated in the seventeenth century with Joshua Poole and John Dryden, who sought to align English with Latin, and it persists mainly as a formal stylistic preference.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the sentence-final preposition as acceptable in everyday speech and writing, with the avoidance guideline framed as a context-sensitive formal-writing convention whose historical origin is documented, not as a grammar rule. Learners are told to judge by register: rephrase in formal academic writing when the alternative reads naturally; otherwise leave the preposition in place.

sourceRecords.title: Prepositions: For Time, Place, and Introducing Objects
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: a preposition is the keyword that starts a prepositional phrase, which ends with the object or noun of the phrase; prepositional phrases act as adverbs or adjectives in that they modify verbs, adverbs, or adjectives; time uses of on (days), at (noon, night, midnight, clock times), and in (parts of the day, months, years, seasons); extended-time prepositions (since, for, by, from-to, during, within). The page's legal notice forbids reproduction without permission, so the lesson uses reference-only facts with original examples.

sourceRecords.title: Prepositions of Location: At, In, On
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: prepositions of location appear with verbs describing states or conditions (especially be) while prepositions of direction appear with verbs of motion; at/in/on can be grouped by the geometry of point, surface, and area or volume. Used reference-only; lesson examples are original.

sourceRecords.title: Prepositions of Direction: To, On (to), In (to)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: to as the basic preposition of direction signifying orientation toward a goal (physical destination, as in 'flew from New York to Paris'); onto as movement toward a surface; into as movement toward the interior of a volume; simple versus compound prepositions and the completion-of-action nuance. Reference only; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Prepositions of place – 'in', 'on', 'at'
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. The live host blocks automated access, so the page (titled 'Prepositions of place – in, on, at') was read via the Internet Archive capture of 2023-09-21 (web.archive.org/web/20230921225728/https://learnenglish.britishcouncil.org/grammar/a1-a2-grammar/prepositions-place; HTTP 200). Supports: in for a place inside a bigger space (box, house, city, country) and other physical locations (in the sea, in the mountains, in a car or taxi); on for surfaces, some public transport (bus, plane, train), lines (rivers, borders, streets) and islands (London is on the River Thames); at for places associated with a specific activity (at work, at school, at a party) and for addresses or exact positions (at 15 Craig Street, at a desk, at the entrance). Facts only; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Prepositions of time – 'at', 'in', 'on'
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. The live host blocks automated access; read via the Internet Archive capture of 2023-06-05 (web.archive.org/web/20230605140615/https://learnenglish.britishcouncil.org/grammar/a1-a2-grammar/prepositions-of-time-at-in-on; HTTP 200). Supports: at with clock times and mealtimes plus phrases such as at night, at the weekend, and at Christmas; in with parts of the day and longer periods (months, seasons, years, centuries, decades); on with days and dates (on Fridays, on 19 October, on New Year's Day). Facts only; lesson examples are original.

sourceRecords.title: Verbs and prepositions
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. The live host blocks automated access; read via the Internet Archive capture of 2023-01-30 (web.archive.org/web/20230130140352/https://learnenglish.britishcouncil.org/grammar/b1-b2-grammar/verbs-and-prepositions; HTTP 200). Supports: when a verb is part of a longer sentence it is often followed by a specific preposition; there are no grammatical rules for which preposition goes with which verb, so verbs and prepositions are best learned together; verifies the collocations depend on ('Their decision will depend on the test results'), listen to ('She listens to the radio a lot'), rely on, agree with, wait for, apologise for, and apply for. Facts only; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Prepositions: uses — English Grammar Today
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: prepositions commonly show a relationship in space or time or a logical relationship between people, places, or things; prepositions are most commonly followed by a noun phrase or pronoun; there are over 100 prepositions in English, with common single-word prepositions including across and through; some pairs and groups of words operate like single prepositions, including out of, in front of, and because of; words such as after and before function as prepositions when followed by a noun phrase and as conjunctions when followed by a clause. Facts only; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Prepositional phrases — English Grammar Today
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200). Supports: prepositional phrases consist of a preposition and the words which follow it (a complement); the complement is most commonly a noun phrase or pronoun, and can also be an adverb phrase, a verb in the -ing form, or a wh-clause (examples: 'They first met at a party'; 'She's decided on doing a Chinese language course'). Facts only; no wording adapted.

sourceRecords.title: Prepositions — Common mistakes in English
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B. Read live on 2026-08-21 (HTTP 200; this slug serves the Common-mistakes hub). Supports: prepositions are a common source of errors because use of prepositions in English differs from that in other languages, and some languages do not use prepositions at all. Used for the learner-mistakes framing; facts only.

sourceRecords.title: Ending a Sentence with a Preposition
sourceRecords.notes: Tier D usage reference. The live host returns HTTP 403 to automated fetch; read via the Internet Archive capture of 2026-08-10 (web.archive.org/web/20260810224838/https://www.merriam-webster.com/grammar/prepositions-ending-a-sentence-with). Supports: ending a sentence with a preposition is permissible in English; the idea that it should be avoided originated with Joshua Poole and John Dryden, who sought to align English with Latin; the idea is still held by many; the technical term preposition stranding; Dryden's 1672 complaint about Ben Jonson. Facts only; no wording adapted.
